NIST, SPUR, RWS, ORP, and Miles’ modeling approach present challenges to communities that desire to increase energy and community resilience but lack significant capacity to 1) identify and process data, 2) develop scenarios for planning, 3) appropriately engage stakeholders and community members at their level of expertise, 4) develop community-based resilience metrics and tracking methodologies, 5) identify strategies and resiliency deployment projects, and 6) provide cost-benefit understanding at multiple scales for plan implementation. The F3 Framework planning process was designed to address the complexity of community energy resilience planning by creation of a framework and tools that incorporate the needs of utilities and governmental entities to inform approaches to renewable-based grid or community assets, while allowing users to participate in defining the critical functions required against multiple outage scenarios at an individual and shared resource level. This process recognizes the “precarious intimacy between energy and the fiscal, social, and technical systems it supports” (Roege 2024), and develops an accessible human-centered design process to inform community energy resilience plans AND effective implementation pathways. Traditional top-down approaches in selecting renewable energy projects neglect to include community impacts and benefits in decision-making. They can also fail in building trust, working towards consensus, and including reciprocity within the local 5 community. In Time as Kinship (Powys 2021), Kyle Powys Whyte writes that “kinship relationships fall under the category of relationships grounded in responsibility.” He continues that “whether faced with a hurricane, a pandemic, or a trade embargo, a high degree of interdependence in the form of shared responsibilities can be a crucial coping strategy.” F3 sought to create trust through a renewable energy planning process that emphasized consensus and included reciprocity of benefits for community members. Learning from past hazard response, forging definitions of minimal resiliency, planning for solar and storage, and iterating amongst both traditional City planning and community-based planning processes, F3 developed a toolkit to guide other capacity-limited Figure 1. communities to engage in deeper resilience F3 iterative framework for combining community expertise with critical systems operators. planning to minimize negative impacts of grid outages. Renewable-based Community Energy Resilience Core strategies in resilience plans include deploying localized power systems at key sites. Planners consistently identify solar PV coupled with battery energy storage as the “typical choice” for off-grid renewably-derived backup power. These systems can operate independently of the grid during outages and provide resilience benefits such as emergency heating, medical-device power, refrigeration, and charging at congregate facilities like shelters or community centers, or at individuals homes or businesses. Although Duluth and many communities generally depend on small diesel backup generators for critical power, studies warn that diesel backups often fail if not regularly tested, making solar and storage a more reliable alternative (Groneman 2024). In cold climates, multi-energy microgrids are also considered. For instance, hybrid systems (e.g. biogas micro-CHP) to co-produce heat and power are being explored to further enhance resiliency in winter.
